claims.text: A thin, compositionally graded, tungsten-rich RHEA interlayer can effectively mediate the mismatch between W and CuCrZr.
Refractory high-entropy alloys can be produced using physical vapor deposition.
Directly bonded W and CuCrZr suffer stress concentrations because of mismatched coefficients of thermal expansion.
Directly bonded W and CuCrZr exhibit poor interfacial bonding and delamination.
Fusion-reactor materials are exposed to high temperature, intense radiation, and mechanical stress.
The relevant W/CuCrZr joint will undergo severe thermal cycling.
A gradual transition in composition and properties between W and CuCrZr will reduce local stress concentrations.
A gradual transition in composition and properties between W and CuCrZr will reduce interfacial delamination.
The RHEA interlayer will provide an intermediate coefficient of thermal expansion that moderates the W/CuCrZr thermal-expansion mismatch.
The RHEA interlayer will improve bonding between W and CuCrZr.
The tailored RHEA interlayer will enhance high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The tailored RHEA interlayer will enhance resistance to radiation damage.
The graded RHEA interlayer will increase mechanical interfacial strength relative to direct W/CuCrZr bonding.
The graded RHEA interlayer will reduce stress concentration and delamination under thermal cycling and irradiation relative to direct W/CuCrZr bonding.
Direct W/CuCrZr bonding produces brittle interfacial phases under extreme operating conditions.
Some RHEA alloying additions can form brittle intermetallic compounds, so composition must be controlled to avoid them.
RHEAs have strong elevated-temperature mechanical properties and are considered promising for high-temperature nuclear applications.
Existing evidence establishes that graded RHEA coatings improve interfacial behavior in W/CuCrZr joints.
